You are an incoming Rice University freshman in summer 2016. You have been randomly assigned to one of the university’s eleven residential colleges and have not yet arrived on campus or experienced college life there. In the current third-party dictator task, decide how to divide $20 between two other incoming freshmen who are participating in this study. One belongs to your own residential college; the other belongs to a different residential college. You do not keep any of this $20. The decision table lists the amount for your own-college recipient first, from $20 down to $0 in $2 steps, with the complementary amount for the other-college recipient alongside it. Everyone first makes a choice as an allocator. After choices, the computer randomly assigns people to the allocator or recipient roles and matches them. If this task is selected for payment and you are the allocator, you receive a fixed $5 for making the decision, regardless of the split, and the two recipients receive the allocation. You may instead be selected as a recipient and receive your share from a matched allocator’s choice. You do not yet know your final role or which tasks will be paid. This phase contains a questionnaire and six incentivized tasks, two of which are randomly chosen for payment at the end. The current allocation follows a preference/personality questionnaire, a standard dictator task and a gambling task. The available aggregate record does not provide your own earlier answers, choices or any task-specific feedback, your residential college name, or individual demographic attributes; it does not imply you were unaware of your own information. How many dollars do you allocate to the person in your own residential college, and how many to the person in a different college?
